body: Google introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen on November 12, 2026, as a speed-focused member of the Gemini 4 family built for everyday coding and agentic workflows. While the frontier models Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon handle deep, long-horizon reasoning on the hardest problems, Hydrogen is positioned as the rapid execution model for the work teams do every day.

Hydrogen launched the same day across Google's developer, enterprise and consumer surfaces: the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, the Gemini app, Google Search, Gemini for business, and Google Antigravity for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. It is also the new default model in Search AI Mode.

The model offers four thinking levels, low, medium, high as the default, and a new xhigh tier, so teams can trade reasoning depth against latency and cost depending on the task instead of paying for maximum reasoning on every request.
content.heading: What Google announced on November 12

body: According to Google, Hydrogen finishes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash at its high default setting, and more than triples Terminal-Bench 4.1 scores, from 18.2 percent to 57 percent. Google also reports that Hydrogen cuts fabricated claims by more than five times compared with the previous Flash model.

On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Google reports Hydrogen scoring 51 against Argon at 50 at its default high thinking level, reaching 54 at the highest xhigh setting. These are vendor-reported benchmark figures, and teams should treat them as directional until they are confirmed against their own workloads.

Pricing is flat across the full 1 million-token context window at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens. Hydrogen supports 1 million tokens of input and up to 1 million tokens of output, which suits long documents, large codebases and multi-file analysis.
content.heading: Speed, price and the benchmarks Google reports

body: Google also introduced Orchestrator in Google Antigravity, which switches between models such as Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session instead of running one model from start to finish. Routine steps can move to Hydrogen while deeper reasoning stays with Carbon.

Google reports that on Terminal-Bench 4.0, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while consuming 24 percent less quota on average and completing work 19 percent faster. For parallel agent work, Carbon can act as coordinator while Hydrogen powers worker and verifier agents that build and test changes at the same time in isolated workspaces.

This split matters for cost control. Execution-heavy steps such as writing code, running tests and verifying changes are where most tokens are spent, so moving them to a faster, cheaper model can cut the bill for an agentic workflow without giving up the frontier model where judgment is needed.
content.heading: The multi-model play: Orchestrator in Antigravity

body: Robby Stein, Google's vice president of product for Search, called Hydrogen the biggest model upgrade to Search yet. Hydrogen is now the default model in AI Mode and is used for the hardest questions in AI Overviews, putting it on two of Google's highest-traffic surfaces from day one rather than in an opt-in tier.

Google says Hydrogen understands questions asked in a natural flow, including questions with multiple parts, hard-to-understand typos and highly specific requests, by breaking a question into its components and answering each part. Responses are also more visual and surface a wider range of relevant links.

Independent testing of the new Search answers was not part of the coverage reviewed for this article, so teams that depend on Search traffic should watch how AI Mode answers and link surfacing behave in practice rather than taking the improvement as measured fact.
content.heading: Search gets its biggest model upgrade

body: Start with a small pilot on execution-heavy work: code review, test runs, bug fixes and verification steps inside an existing repository. Measure completion time, token spend and defect rates against the current setup before widening the rollout.

Keep frontier models for architecture decisions, subtle bugs and long-horizon reasoning, and let Hydrogen handle the high-volume steps. That split mirrors how Google positions the family, and it is the fastest way to see whether the speed and price advantage holds on real code.

Finally, check the rollout surfaces your team already uses. Hydrogen is available through the Gemini API and AI Studio, so an existing integration can try it without a platform change, and teams building AI agents or automation can test whether a faster execution model improves their own workflows.

body: Nvidia has a new face at the top for the first time in a generation. Jensen Huang, who led the company for 33 years and turned a graphics-chip maker into the most important supplier of the AI era, has resigned as chief executive, president and board member. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim chief executive while the board searches for a permanent successor.

Reports say the resignation followed a board investigation and reports about Huang's personal conduct, including allegations involving a woman suspected of passing information to China. Nvidia has not presented the departure as a strategy change, and the company continues to operate under its existing leadership team, but the sudden exit of the executive most associated with the AI boom has put the company under unusual scrutiny.
content.heading: What happened at Nvidia

body: Nvidia's chips sit at the centre of almost every serious AI effort. Training a frontier model, running a large chatbot, or building an AI agent platform usually means buying, renting or queuing for Nvidia accelerators, and many teams plan their budgets and product launches around Nvidia's roadmap and supply. A leadership change at the top therefore reaches far beyond one company's boardroom: it raises questions about pricing, allocation, product timing and how aggressively the company will keep investing in new chip generations.

That does not mean supply stops or roadmaps are cancelled. Nvidia's engineering teams, manufacturing partners and customer commitments remain in place, and Kress has worked alongside Huang for years as chief financial officer, so she knows the company's customers, costs and supply chain. The practical question for buyers is not whether Nvidia disappears, but whether decisions slow down while the company is run by an interim chief.
content.heading: Why the change matters for AI teams

body: Investors have reacted sharply to the uncertainty. Reports put Nvidia's loss of market value at more than one trillion dollars since the first revelations in late October, a scale of decline that shows how much of the AI trade was tied to confidence in one leader. At the same time, the wider AI buildout has not paused: in the same week, SpaceX disclosed plans to invest more than 74 billion dollars in AI supercomputing campuses, and Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a faster model built for coding and AI agents.

The contrast matters. The demand for computing power keeps growing even while the company that supplies most of it goes through a leadership crisis, which suggests the pressure on chip supply and data-centre capacity will continue whatever Nvidia's board decides next.
content.heading: The market reaction so far

body: For teams buying AI infrastructure or building products on top of it, the sensible response is planning, not panic. Confirm current allocations and delivery dates with suppliers rather than assuming they will slip, and keep a second option warm where a project depends on a single chip family or cloud provider. A leadership transition is also a good moment to review contracts: check what happens to pricing and support if a roadmap date moves, and make sure long-term commitments have room for change.

Watch two signals in the coming weeks. The first is the permanent chief executive appointment, which will show whether the board wants continuity or a new direction. The second is Nvidia's next guidance on sales and supply, which will show whether the leadership change has affected the business or only the share price. Until those arrive, projects should continue as planned, with a little more attention paid to supply risk than usual.
content.heading: What buyers and builders should do now

body: The episode is a reminder that the AI boom still depends on a small number of companies and people. One resignation has moved markets, raised geopolitical questions and forced customers to rethink their plans, all in a single week. For businesses, the lesson is to treat AI supply like any other critical dependency: understand where it comes from, keep alternatives ready, and avoid building a strategy that collapses if one supplier or one leader changes.

Nvidia will almost certainly remain central to AI computing, whoever leads it next. The company's technology, customer base and manufacturing scale do not change overnight. But the week has shown that leadership risk is now part of AI planning, and the teams that plan for it will be the ones least affected when the next surprise arrives.
content.heading: The bigger lesson for the AI industry
